# Solutions: Part II {#sec-solutions-part-2}

Solutions to the exercises in Part II, grouped by chapter, followed by the solutions to the Part II review. Try each exercise before reading its solution. The link after each solution takes you back to its exercise.

## Systems of linear equations {#sec-solutions-linear-systems}

Exercises from @sec-linear-systems.

[**1.**]{#solution-linear-systems-1}
$$
\M{A} = \mat{3 & 0 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & -1},
$$
$$
\vect{x} = \mat{x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3},
$$
$$
\vect{b} = \mat{4 \\ 0 \\ 5},
$$
and the augmented matrix is $\amat{rrr|r}{3 & 0 & -2 & 4 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -1 & 5}$. A missing unknown has coefficient 0.

[Back to exercise 1](../part-2/10-linear-systems.qmd#exercise-linear-systems-1){.sol-link}

[**2.**]{#solution-linear-systems-2}

(a) From the second equation, $y = 3x - 5$. Substituting into the first, $x + 6x - 10 = 4$, so $x = 2$ and $y = 1$. The lines cross once, at $(2, 1)$.

(b) The second equation is $-\tfrac{1}{2}$ times the first, so both describe the same line, $x - 2y = 3$. There are infinitely many solutions: $x = 3 + 2t$, $y = t$ for any $t$.

(c) Doubling the first equation gives $2x - 2y = 2$, which contradicts $2x - 2y = 5$. The lines are parallel (both have slope 1) and there is no solution.

[Back to exercise 2](../part-2/10-linear-systems.qmd#exercise-linear-systems-2){.sol-link}

[**3.**]{#solution-linear-systems-3} The system is $x\mat{1 \\ 3} + y\mat{2 \\ -1} = \mat{4 \\ 5}$, and indeed $2\mat{1 \\ 3} + 1\mat{2 \\ -1} = \mat{4 \\ 5}$.

[Back to exercise 3](../part-2/10-linear-systems.qmd#exercise-linear-systems-3){.sol-link}

[**4.**]{#solution-linear-systems-4} The coefficient matrix has determinant $6 - 3k$, which is zero only when $k = 2$.

(a) For $k \neq 2$ there is exactly one solution, whatever $c$ is.

(b), (c) For $k = 2$ the equations are $x + 2y = 2$ and $3x + 6y = c$. Three times the first is $3x + 6y = 6$. So if $c = 6$ the two equations describe the same line and there are infinitely many solutions; if $c \neq 6$ they are parallel lines and there is no solution.

[Back to exercise 4](../part-2/10-linear-systems.qmd#exercise-linear-systems-4){.sol-link}

[**5.**]{#solution-linear-systems-5}

(a) $\M{A}(s\vect{h}_1 + t\vect{h}_2) = s\M{A}\vect{h}_1 + t\M{A}\vect{h}_2 = s\zerovec + t\zerovec = \zerovec$.

(b) $\M{A}(\vect{p} + \vect{h}) = \M{A}\vect{p} + \M{A}\vect{h} = \vect{b} + \zerovec = \vect{b}$.

(c) $\M{A}(\vect{q} - \vect{p}) = \M{A}\vect{q} - \M{A}\vect{p} = \vect{b} - \vect{b} = \zerovec$.

Part (b) shows that every vector $\vect{p} + \vect{h}$ is a solution. Part (c) shows that every solution $\vect{q}$ is of this form, with $\vect{h} = \vect{q} - \vect{p}$. Together they say that the solutions are exactly the vectors $\vect{p} + \vect{h}$.

[Back to exercise 5](../part-2/10-linear-systems.qmd#exercise-linear-systems-5){.sol-link}

[**6.**]{#solution-linear-systems-6} Carbon: $3a = c$. Hydrogen: $8a = 2d$. Oxygen: $2b = 2c + d$. Taking $a = 1$ gives $c = 3$ and $d = 4$, and then $2b = 6 + 4$, so $b = 5$:
$$
\mathrm{C_3H_8} + 5\,\mathrm{O_2} \longrightarrow 3\,\mathrm{CO_2} + 4\,\mathrm{H_2O}.
$$

[Back to exercise 6](../part-2/10-linear-systems.qmd#exercise-linear-systems-6){.sol-link}

[**7.**]{#solution-linear-systems-7} Some of the possibilities:

(a) One solution: three planes meeting at a single point, like the floor and two walls in the corner of a room.

(b) A line of solutions: three different planes through one line, like pages of a book; or two equations describing the same plane, with the third plane crossing it.

(c) A plane of solutions: all three equations describe the same plane.

(d) No solution: two parallel planes (the third can be anything); three parallel planes; two equations describing the same plane, with the third parallel to it; or a triangular tube, where each pair of planes meets in a line but the three lines are parallel.

[Back to exercise 7](../part-2/10-linear-systems.qmd#exercise-linear-systems-7){.sol-link}

[**8.**]{#solution-linear-systems-8}

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
import numpy as np

A = np.array([[0.6, 0.8, 0.5],
              [0.3, 0.1, 0.2],
              [0.1, 0.1, 0.3]])
print(np.linalg.solve(A, [65, 20, 15]))
print(np.linalg.solve(A, [55, 30, 15]))
```

## MATLAB

```matlab
A = [0.6 0.8 0.5; 0.3 0.1 0.2; 0.1 0.1 0.3];
x1 = A \ [65; 20; 15]
x2 = A \ [55; 30; 15]
```

```{.text .code-output}
x1 =

   37.5000
   37.5000
   25.0000

x2 =

   87.5000
  -12.5000
   25.0000
```
:::

The first alloy needs 37.5 kg of alloy 1, 37.5 kg of alloy 2 and 25 kg of alloy 3. The second "needs" $-12.5$ kg of alloy 2, which is impossible: the workshop can't add a negative amount. The equations have a solution, but it has no physical meaning, so this alloy can't be made from these three scraps. In the column picture, $\vect{b}$ can be made from the columns, but not with amounts that are all positive.

## Gaussian elimination {#sec-solutions-gaussian-elimination}

Exercises from @sec-gaussian-elimination.

[**1.**]{#solution-gaussian-elimination-1} Eliminate column 1 with $R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - 2R_1$ and $R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - R_1$, then column 2 with $R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - R_2$:

$$
\amat{rrr|r}{1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 & 11 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 & 14}
\to
\amat{rrr|r}{1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 8}
\to
\amat{rrr|r}{1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & 9}.
$$

Back substitution gives $z = 3$, then $y - 3 = -1$ so $y = 2$, then $x + 2 + 3 = 6$ so $x = 1$.

[Back to exercise 1](../part-2/11-gaussian-elimination.qmd#exercise-gaussian-elimination-1){.sol-link}

[**2.**]{#solution-gaussian-elimination-2} With $R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - R_1$ and $R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - 2R_1$, then $R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - R_2$:

$$
\amat{rrr|r}{1 & 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 & 5 \\ 2 & 3 & 4 & 8}
\to
\amat{rrr|r}{1 & 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 4}
\to
\amat{rrr|r}{1 & 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1}.
$$

The last row says $0 = 1$, so there is no solution. Geometrically, each pair of planes meets in a line, but the three lines are parallel, so no point lies on all three planes. (The third plane's normal is the sum of the other two, which is why the lines are parallel.)

[Back to exercise 2](../part-2/11-gaussian-elimination.qmd#exercise-gaussian-elimination-2){.sol-link}

[**3.**]{#solution-gaussian-elimination-3} The same steps now end with the row $\amat{ccc|c}{0 & 0 & 0 & 0}$, which places no restriction. The remaining rows say $y + 2z = 3$ and $x + y + z = 2$. Taking $z$ as a free parameter,

$$
y = 3 - 2z,
$$
$$
x = 2 - y - z = -1 + z,
$$

so the solutions are $\vect{x} = \mat{-1 + z \\ 3 - 2z \\ z}$ for any number $z$. They form a line: all three planes meet along it.

[Back to exercise 3](../part-2/11-gaussian-elimination.qmd#exercise-gaussian-elimination-3){.sol-link}

[**4.**]{#solution-gaussian-elimination-4} The first pivot is $a_{11} = 0$, and the function divides by it, so it stops with an error. The system itself is fine: swapping the rows gives

$$
\amat{rr|r}{1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1},
$$

so $y = 1$ and $x = 1$. Row swaps like this are the subject of @sec-pivoting.

[Back to exercise 4](../part-2/11-gaussian-elimination.qmd#exercise-gaussian-elimination-4){.sol-link}

[**5.**]{#solution-gaussian-elimination-5} The pivots were $2$, $\tfrac{1}{2}$ and $-1$, and no rows were swapped, so $\det\M{A} = 2 \times \tfrac{1}{2} \times (-1) = -1$. (Adding multiples of rows doesn't change the determinant, and the final matrix is triangular.) By cofactor expansion along the first row,
$$
\det\M{A} = 2\begin{vmatrix} -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \end{vmatrix} - 1\begin{vmatrix} -3 & 2 \\ -2 & 2 \end{vmatrix} + (-1)\begin{vmatrix} -3 & -1 \\ -2 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 2(-4) - (-2) - (-5) = -1. \;✓
$$

[Back to exercise 5](../part-2/11-gaussian-elimination.qmd#exercise-gaussian-elimination-5){.sol-link}

[**6.**]{#solution-gaussian-elimination-6} One way to count operations:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
import numpy as np

def elimination_count(A, b):
    """Gaussian elimination that also counts arithmetic operations."""
    A = np.array(A, dtype=float)
    b = np.array(b, dtype=float)
    n = len(b)
    ops = 0
    for k in range(n - 1):
        for i in range(k + 1, n):
            m = A[i, k] / A[k, k]
            A[i, k:] -= m * A[k, k:]
            b[i] -= m * b[k]
            ops += 1 + 2 * (n - k) + 2      # divide, row update, right-hand side
    x = np.zeros(n)
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        x[i] = (b[i] - A[i, i + 1:] @ x[i + 1:]) / A[i, i]
        ops += 2 * (n - i - 1) + 2          # dot product, subtract, divide
    return x, ops

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
for n in [10, 20, 40, 80]:
    _, ops = elimination_count(rng.standard_normal((n, n)), rng.standard_normal(n))
    print(f"n = {n:3d}   operations = {ops:7d}   2n^3/3 = {2 * n**3 / 3:9.0f}   ratio = {ops / (2 * n**3 / 3):.2f}")
```

## MATLAB

```matlab
for n = [10 20 40 80]
    [~, ops] = elimination_count(randn(n), randn(n,1));
    fprintf('n = %3d   operations = %7d   2n^3/3 = %9.0f   ratio = %.2f\n', ...
            n, ops, 2*n^3/3, ops/(2*n^3/3));
end

function [x, ops] = elimination_count(A, b)
% Gaussian elimination that also counts arithmetic operations.
n = length(b);
ops = 0;
for k = 1:n-1
    for i = k+1:n
        m = A(i,k) / A(k,k);
        A(i,k:n) = A(i,k:n) - m * A(k,k:n);
        b(i) = b(i) - m * b(k);
        ops = ops + 1 + 2*(n-k+1) + 2;   % divide, row update, right-hand side
    end
end
x = zeros(n,1);
for i = n:-1:1
    x(i) = (b(i) - A(i,i+1:n) * x(i+1:n)) / A(i,i);
    ops = ops + 2*(n-i) + 2;             % dot product, subtract, divide
end
end
```
:::

The ratio approaches 1 as $n$ grows. For small systems the lower-order terms, such as the $n^2$ operations of back substitution, still matter.

[Back to exercise 6](../part-2/11-gaussian-elimination.qmd#exercise-gaussian-elimination-6){.sol-link}

## Gauss–Jordan elimination and rank {#sec-solutions-gauss-jordan-rank}

Exercises from @sec-gauss-jordan-rank.

[**1.**]{#solution-gauss-jordan-rank-1}

(a) Reduced row echelon form.

(b) Neither: the row of zeros is not at the bottom. Swapping rows 2 and 3 gives reduced row echelon form.

(c) Row echelon form, but not reduced: the pivot in row 2 is in column 3, and the 5 above it should be 0.

(d) Reduced row echelon form.

[Back to exercise 1](../part-2/12-gauss-jordan-rank.qmd#exercise-gauss-jordan-rank-1){.sol-link}

[**2.**]{#solution-gauss-jordan-rank-2} $R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - 2R_1$ and $R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - 3R_1$ give rows $(1, 2, 1)$, $(0, 0, 1)$ and $(0, 0, 1)$. Column 2 has no pivot. Then $R_1 \leftarrow R_1 - R_2$ and $R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - R_2$ give
$$
\mat{1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0},
$$
with rank 2.

[Back to exercise 2](../part-2/12-gauss-jordan-rank.qmd#exercise-gauss-jordan-rank-2){.sol-link}

[**3.**]{#solution-gauss-jordan-rank-3} $R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - 2R_1$ gives $\amat{rrr|r}{1 & -1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1}$, and $R_1 \leftarrow R_1 - 2R_2$ gives the reduced form $\amat{rrr|r}{1 & -1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1}$. The pivot variables are $x_1$ and $x_3$, and $x_2 = s$ is free. So $x_3 = 1$ and $x_1 = 1 + s$:
$$
\vect{x} = \mat{1 \\ 0 \\ 1} + s\mat{1 \\ 1 \\ 0}.
$$

[Back to exercise 3](../part-2/12-gauss-jordan-rank.qmd#exercise-gauss-jordan-rank-3){.sol-link}

[**4.**]{#solution-gauss-jordan-rank-4} For the $2 \times 2$ matrix:
$$
\amat{rr|rr}{2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 5 & 3 & 0 & 1}
\xrightarrow{R_2 \,\leftarrow\, R_2 - \frac{5}{2}R_1}
\amat{rr|rr}{2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \tfrac{1}{2} & -\tfrac{5}{2} & 1}
\xrightarrow{R_2 \,\leftarrow\, 2R_2}
\amat{rr|rr}{2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -5 & 2}
$$
$$
\xrightarrow{R_1 \,\leftarrow\, R_1 - R_2}
\amat{rr|rr}{2 & 0 & 6 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & -5 & 2}
\xrightarrow{R_1 \,\leftarrow\, \frac{1}{2}R_1}
\amat{rr|rr}{1 & 0 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -5 & 2},
$$
so the inverse is $\mat{3 & -1 \\ -5 & 2}$. (This agrees with the $2 \times 2$ formula, since the determinant is 1.)

For the $3 \times 3$ matrix, $R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - 2R_1$ gives row 2 as $(0, 1, -1)$ on the left, and then $R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - R_2$ makes the left part of row 3 all zeros. Column 3 has no pivot, so the left half can never become $\M{I}$, and the matrix has no inverse. (Its rank is 2, and its determinant is 0.)

[Back to exercise 4](../part-2/12-gauss-jordan-rank.qmd#exercise-gauss-jordan-rank-4){.sol-link}

[**5.**]{#solution-gauss-jordan-rank-5} Eliminating gives
$$
\amat{rrr|c}{1 & 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & a & b}
\xrightarrow[R_3 \,\leftarrow\, R_3 - 2R_1]{R_2 \,\leftarrow\, R_2 - R_1}
\amat{rrr|c}{1 & 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & a - 2 & b - 4}
\xrightarrow{R_3 \,\leftarrow\, R_3 - R_2}
\amat{rrr|c}{1 & 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & a & b - 3}.
$$

(a) If $a \neq 0$, there are three pivots: exactly one solution.

(b) If $a = 0$ and $b \neq 3$, the last row says $0 = b - 3 \neq 0$: no solution.

(c) If $a = 0$ and $b = 3$, the last row is all zeros: rank 2, with one free variable, so infinitely many solutions.

[Back to exercise 5](../part-2/12-gauss-jordan-rank.qmd#exercise-gauss-jordan-rank-5){.sol-link}

[**6.**]{#solution-gauss-jordan-rank-6} With $m$ equations and $n > m$ unknowns, there is at most one pivot per row, so the rank is at most $m$, and there are at least $n - m \ge 1$ free variables. A homogeneous system is always consistent, so we can set one free variable to 1 (and any others to 0), and solve for the pivot variables. That gives a solution with a non-zero entry.

[Back to exercise 6](../part-2/12-gauss-jordan-rank.qmd#exercise-gauss-jordan-rank-6){.sol-link}

[**7.**]{#solution-gauss-jordan-rank-7} The balances are: carbon, $a = 6c$; hydrogen, $2b = 12c$; oxygen, $2a + b = 6c + 2d$. As a homogeneous system in $a, b, c, d$:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
import numpy as np

def rref(M, tol=1e-10):
    R = np.array(M, dtype=float)
    m, n = R.shape
    pivots, r = [], 0
    for c in range(n):
        if r == m:
            break
        p = r + np.argmax(abs(R[r:, c]))
        if abs(R[p, c]) < tol:
            continue
        R[[r, p]] = R[[p, r]]
        R[r] /= R[r, c]
        for i in range(m):
            if i != r:
                R[i] -= R[i, c] * R[r]
        pivots.append(c)
        r += 1
    return R, pivots

M = [[1, 0, -6, 0],      # carbon
     [0, 2, -12, 0],     # hydrogen
     [2, 1, -6, -2]]     # oxygen
R, piv = rref(M)
print(np.round(R, 4) + 0)
```

## MATLAB

```matlab
M = [1 0 -6 0;           % carbon
     0 2 -12 0;          % hydrogen
     2 1 -6 -2];         % oxygen
rref(M)
```

```{.text .code-output}
ans =

    1.0000         0         0   -1.0000
         0    1.0000         0   -1.0000
         0         0    1.0000   -0.1667
```
:::

The free variable is $d$, and the rows say $a = d$, $b = d$ and $c = d/6$. The smallest whole numbers come from $d = 6$:
$$
6\,\mathrm{CO_2} + 6\,\mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6} + 6\,\mathrm{O_2}.
$$

[Back to exercise 7](../part-2/12-gauss-jordan-rank.qmd#exercise-gauss-jordan-rank-7){.sol-link}

## LU decomposition {#sec-solutions-lu-decomposition}

Exercises from @sec-lu-decomposition.

[**1.**]{#solution-lu-decomposition-1}

(a) The multiplier is $m_{21} = 3$, and $R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - 3R_1$ gives $(0, 2)$. So
$$
\M{L} = \mat{1 & 0 \\ 3 & 1},
$$
$$
\M{U} = \mat{1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2}.
$$

(b) The multipliers are $m_{21} = 2$ and $m_{31} = 3$, giving rows $(0, 1, 2)$ and $(0, 2, 5)$, then $m_{32} = 2$, giving $(0, 0, 1)$. So
$$
\M{L} = \mat{1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 2 & 1},
$$
$$
\M{U} = \mat{1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1}.
$$
Multiplying out $\M{L}\M{U}$ gives back $\M{A}$ in both cases.

[Back to exercise 1](../part-2/13-lu-decomposition.qmd#exercise-lu-decomposition-1){.sol-link}

[**2.**]{#solution-lu-decomposition-2} For $\vect{b} = (3, 9, 16)\T$: forward substitution gives $y_1 = 3$, $y_2 = 9 - 2(3) = 3$, $y_3 = 16 - 3(3) - 2(3) = 1$. Back substitution gives $x_3 = 1$, $x_2 = 3 - 2(1) = 1$, $x_1 = 3 - 1 - 1 = 1$. So $\vect{x} = (1, 1, 1)\T$.

For $\vect{b} = (0, 1, 3)\T$: $y_1 = 0$, $y_2 = 1$, $y_3 = 3 - 0 - 2(1) = 1$; then $x_3 = 1$, $x_2 = 1 - 2 = -1$, $x_1 = 0 - (-1) - 1 = 0$. So $\vect{x} = (0, -1, 1)\T$.

[Back to exercise 2](../part-2/13-lu-decomposition.qmd#exercise-lu-decomposition-2){.sol-link}

[**3.**]{#solution-lu-decomposition-3} A general product of this shape is
$$
\mat{1 & 0 \\ \ell & 1}\mat{u_{11} & u_{12} \\ 0 & u_{22}} = \mat{u_{11} & u_{12} \\ \ell u_{11} & \ell u_{12} + u_{22}}.
$$
For this to equal $\mat{0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1}$, the top-left entries need $u_{11} = 0$, but then the bottom-left entry is $\ell u_{11} = 0$, not 1. So there is no such factorisation. Swapping the rows, with $\M{P} = \mat{0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0}$, gives $\M{P}\M{A} = \mat{1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1}$, which is already upper triangular: $\M{L} = \M{I}$ and $\M{U} = \mat{1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1}$.

[Back to exercise 3](../part-2/13-lu-decomposition.qmd#exercise-lu-decomposition-3){.sol-link}

[**4.**]{#solution-lu-decomposition-4} No rows were swapped, so $\det\M{A} = \det\M{L}\,\det\M{U} = 1 \times (1 \times 1 \times 1) = 1$. $\M{L}$ is triangular, so its determinant is the product of its diagonal entries, which are all 1.

[Back to exercise 4](../part-2/13-lu-decomposition.qmd#exercise-lu-decomposition-4){.sol-link}

[**5.**]{#solution-lu-decomposition-5}

(a) $50 \times \tfrac{2}{3} \times 2000^3 \approx 50 \times 5.3 \times 10^9 \approx 2.7 \times 10^{11}$ operations.

(b) One factorisation, about $5.3 \times 10^9$ operations, plus 50 pairs of triangular solves, about $50 \times 2 \times 2000^2 = 4 \times 10^8$. The total is about $5.7 \times 10^9$, so (b) is roughly 47 times faster.

[Back to exercise 5](../part-2/13-lu-decomposition.qmd#exercise-lu-decomposition-5){.sol-link}

[**6.**]{#solution-lu-decomposition-6} Let $\M{L}$ and $\M{M}$ be lower triangular, so $\ell_{ik} = 0$ when $k > i$ and $m_{kj} = 0$ when $k < j$. The $(i, j)$ entry of $\M{L}\M{M}$ is $\sum_k \ell_{ik} m_{kj}$. If $i < j$, every term has either $k > i$ (so $\ell_{ik} = 0$) or $k \le i < j$ (so $m_{kj} = 0$). So every entry above the diagonal is zero, and $\M{L}\M{M}$ is lower triangular.

[Back to exercise 6](../part-2/13-lu-decomposition.qmd#exercise-lu-decomposition-6){.sol-link}

[**7.**]{#solution-lu-decomposition-7}

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
import numpy as np

def forward_substitution(L, b):
    """Solve Ly = b, for L lower triangular with 1s on its diagonal."""
    n = len(b)
    y = np.zeros(n)
    for i in range(n):
        y[i] = b[i] - L[i, :i] @ y[:i]
    return y

def back_substitution(U, y):
    """Solve Ux = y, for U upper triangular."""
    n = len(y)
    x = np.zeros(n)
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        x[i] = (y[i] - U[i, i + 1:] @ x[i + 1:]) / U[i, i]
    return x

L = np.array([[1, 0, 0], [2, 1, 0], [3, 2, 1]])
U = np.array([[1, 1, 1], [0, 1, 2], [0, 0, 1]])
A = L @ U
for b in ([3, 9, 16], [0, 1, 3]):
    x = back_substitution(U, forward_substitution(L, b))
    print(x, np.allclose(x, np.linalg.solve(A, b)))
```

## MATLAB

```matlab
L = [1 0 0; 2 1 0; 3 2 1];
U = [1 1 1; 0 1 2; 0 0 1];
A = L * U;
b = [3; 9; 16];
x = U \ forward_substitution(L, b)
norm(x - A \ b)              % zero: the answers agree

function y = forward_substitution(L, b)
% Solve Ly = b, for L lower triangular with 1s on its diagonal.
n = length(b);
y = zeros(n, 1);
for i = 1:n
    y(i) = b(i) - L(i, 1:i-1) * y(1:i-1);
end
end
```


## Part II review {#sec-solutions-review-2}

Exercises from the [Part II review](../part-2/review.qmd).

[**1.**]{#solution-review-2-1} *Uses @sec-gaussian-elimination and @sec-determinants.* Subtract 2 × row 1 from row 2 and row 1 from row 3, then subtract the new row 2 from row 3:
$$
\amat{rrr|r}{1 & 2 & 1 & 4 \\ 2 & 5 & 3 & 10 \\ 1 & 3 & 4 & 8}
\to
\amat{rrr|r}{1 & 2 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 4}
\to
\amat{rrr|r}{1 & 2 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2}.
$$
Back substitution gives $z = 1$, $y = 2 - 1 = 1$ and $x = 4 - 2 - 1 = 1$. Adding a multiple of one row to another doesn't change the determinant, so $\det\M{A}$ is the product of the pivots, $1 \times 1 \times 2 = 2$.

[Back to exercise 1](../part-2/review.qmd#exercise-review-2-1){.sol-link}

[**2.**]{#solution-review-2-2} *Uses @sec-gaussian-elimination, @sec-gauss-jordan-rank and @sec-linear-systems.* Elimination gives
$$
\amat{rrr|r}{1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & a - 4 & b - 3}.
$$

- (i) If $a \neq 4$, there are three pivots, and exactly one solution. The three planes meet at a single point.
- (ii) If $a = 4$ and $b \neq 3$, the last row says $0 = b - 3 \neq 0$, so there is no solution. No two of the planes are parallel (their normals $(1, 1, 1)$, $(1, 2, 3)$ and $(2, 3, 4)$ are not multiples of each other), so they meet in pairs along three parallel lines, like the sides of a triangular tent.
- (iii) If $a = 4$ and $b = 3$, the last row is all zeros, and
  $$\amat{rrr|r}{1 & 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0}.$$
  $z$ is free: $x = t$, $y = 1 - 2t$, $z = t$. The three planes share a common line.

[Back to exercise 2](../part-2/review.qmd#exercise-review-2-2){.sol-link}

[**3.**]{#solution-review-2-3} *Uses @sec-gauss-jordan-rank, @sec-inverses and @sec-determinants.* Row reduce $[\,\M{A} \mid \M{I}\,]$: $R_3 - R_1$, then $R_3 + 2R_2$, then $R_3 \div 3$, then $R_2 - R_3$, then $R_1 - 2R_2$, which gives
$$
\M{A}^{-1} = \frac{1}{3}\mat{1 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 & 1}.
$$
Expanding along the first row, $\det\M{A} = 1(1 - 0) - 2(0 - 1) + 0 = 3$, which matches the $\tfrac{1}{3}$ in front (the inverse is the adjugate divided by the determinant). Multiplying out, $\M{A}\M{A}^{-1} = \M{I}$. Then
$$\vect{x} = \M{A}^{-1}\mat{1 \\ 1 \\ 1} = \frac{1}{3}\mat{1 \\ 1 \\ 2}.$$

[Back to exercise 3](../part-2/review.qmd#exercise-review-2-3){.sol-link}

[**4.**]{#solution-review-2-4} *Uses @sec-lu-decomposition and @sec-determinants.* The multipliers are $\ell_{21} = 2$ and $\ell_{31} = 4$, which leave rows $(0, 1, 1)$ and $(0, 3, 5)$, and then $\ell_{32} = 3$, which leaves $(0, 0, 2)$:
$$
\M{L} = \mat{1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 4 & 3 & 1}, \qquad
\M{U} = \mat{2 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2}.
$$
$\det\M{A} = \det\M{L}\det\M{U} = 1 \times (2 \times 1 \times 2) = 4$. Forward substitution in $\M{L}\vect{y} = (4, 10, 24)\T$ gives $y_1 = 4$, $y_2 = 10 - 8 = 2$ and $y_3 = 24 - 16 - 6 = 2$. Back substitution in $\M{U}\vect{x} = \vect{y}$ gives $x_3 = 1$, $x_2 = 2 - 1 = 1$ and $x_1 = (4 - 1 - 1)/2 = 1$.

[Back to exercise 4](../part-2/review.qmd#exercise-review-2-4){.sol-link}

[**5.**]{#solution-review-2-5} *Uses @sec-gauss-jordan-rank and @sec-linear-systems.* $\vect{a}_3 = \vect{a}_1 + \vect{a}_2$, and $\vect{a}_1$ and $\vect{a}_2$ are not parallel, so the rank is 2. The columns span a plane: every combination $x\vect{a}_1 + y\vect{a}_2 = (x, x + y, y)$ has its middle entry equal to the sum of the other two.

- $(1, 0, 1)$ fails this test ($1 + 1 \neq 0$), so it is not a combination of the columns. Elimination on the augmented matrix gives a row $(0, 0, 0 \mid c)$ with $c \neq 0$, so the augmented matrix has rank 3, more than the rank of $\M{A}$.
- $(1, 3, 2)$ passes ($1 + 2 = 3$): it is $\vect{a}_1 + 2\vect{a}_2$. The augmented matrix also has rank 2, so the system is consistent, with one free variable since the rank is less than 3.

[Back to exercise 5](../part-2/review.qmd#exercise-review-2-5){.sol-link}

[**6.**]{#solution-review-2-6} *Uses @sec-linear-systems and @sec-gauss-jordan-rank.* Counting atoms of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen on each side:
$$
3a = c, \qquad 8a = 2d, \qquad 2b = 2c + d.
$$
This is the homogeneous system
$$
\mat{3 & 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 8 & 0 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -2 & -1}\mat{a \\ b \\ c \\ d} = \zerovec,
$$
whose matrix has rank 3, so there is one free variable. Taking $a = 1$ gives $c = 3$, $d = 4$ and $b = (6 + 4)/2 = 5$:
$$\mathrm{C_3H_8} + 5\,\mathrm{O_2} \to 3\,\mathrm{CO_2} + 4\,\mathrm{H_2O}.$$

[Back to exercise 6](../part-2/review.qmd#exercise-review-2-6){.sol-link}

[**7.**]{#solution-review-2-7} *Uses @sec-lu-decomposition.* The factorisation costs about $\tfrac{2}{3}n^3$ operations, so multiplying $n$ by 4 multiplies the time by $4^3 = 64$: about $64 \times 0.2 = 12.8$ seconds. With the factors kept, each extra right-hand side needs only forward and back substitution, about $2n^2$ operations, which is $3/n$ of the factorisation: about $12.8 \times 3/4000 \approx 0.01$ seconds each, or roughly half a second for all 50. Starting again each time would take $50 \times 12.8 = 640$ seconds, over ten minutes.

[Back to exercise 7](../part-2/review.qmd#exercise-review-2-7){.sol-link}

[**8.**]{#solution-review-2-8} *Uses @sec-lu-decomposition and @sec-inverses.*

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
import numpy as np
import scipy.linalg as sl

A = np.array([[2.0, 1, 1], [4, 3, 3], [8, 7, 9]])
f = sl.lu_factor(A)                       # factorise once
print(sl.lu_solve(f, [4, 10, 24]))

# Solving for e1, e2 and e3 gives the columns of the inverse
A_inv = np.column_stack([sl.lu_solve(f, e) for e in np.eye(3)])
print(np.round(A_inv, 4))
print("Agrees with inv(A):", np.allclose(A_inv, np.linalg.inv(A)))
```

## MATLAB

```matlab
A = [2 1 1; 4 3 3; 8 7 9];
[L, U, P] = lu(A);               % P*A = L*U, factorised once
solve = @(b) U \ (L \ (P*b));    % each solve is two triangular solves
fprintf('x = %g %g %g\n', solve([4; 10; 24]))
I = eye(3);
Ainv = [solve(I(:,1)), solve(I(:,2)), solve(I(:,3))]
fprintf('Agrees with inv(A): %d\n', norm(Ainv - inv(A)) < 1e-12)
```

```{.text .code-output}
x = 1 1 1
Ainv =

    1.5000   -0.5000         0
   -3.0000    2.5000   -0.5000
    1.0000   -1.5000    0.5000

Agrees with inv(A): 1
```
:::

This is how software finds an inverse when one is really needed: one factorisation, then one cheap solve per column.
